titulo: NATO – How the Atlantic Alliance works
pergunta: How was NATO created, how does it work today, and what is the impact of this alliance on Brazil's defense policies?
emUmaFrase: NATO was born in 1949 as a collective defense alliance between North America and Europe; today it operates as an integrated military organization that guarantees collective security and influences, albeit in a limited way, Brazil's defense policies.
paraComecar:
The North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) emerged shortly after World War II, when twelve countries – United States, Canada, United Kingdom, France, Italy, Portugal, Norway, Denmark, Iceland, Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg – signed the North Atlantic Treaty on April 4, 1949. The goal was to create a collective defense system: an attack on any member would be considered an attack on all, according to Article 5 of the treaty.

During the Cold War, NATO consolidated its military structure under the leadership of North‑American commanders and became the main barrier against the expansion of the Soviet Union and the Warsaw Pact. After the fall of the Berlin Wall, the alliance began to intervene in conflicts outside Europe, such as Bosnia (1992‑1995), Kosovo (1999) and Libya (2011), in addition to leading the mission in Afghanistan after the September 11, 2001 attacks.

Today NATO has 32 member states, headquartered in Brussels, Belgium, and maintains a joint budget of about €5 billion (2026). Each country must allocate at least 2 % of GDP to defense, and the alliance accounts for more than 55 % of global military spending. Besides collective defense, NATO develops partnerships for peace, training programs and cooperation in cyber security.

In Brazil, although it is not a member, NATO influences defense policy by setting interoperability standards, promoting joint exercises and offering training courses for Brazilian military personnel. This relationship reinforces the modernization of the Armed Forces, but the direct impact remains limited, as Brazil follows its own defense strategy based on bilateral agreements and its participation in regional organizations such as UNASUR and the Strategic Partnership with the United States.

historiaIdeia: NATO was born out of the Cold War for collective defense and today operates in global security, influencing Brazil's defense policy.
historia:
NATO emerged shortly after World War II, when the Dunkirk Treaty (1947) and the Brussels Treaty (1948) paved the way for the alliance. On 4 April 1949, twelve countries signed the North Atlantic Treaty, creating the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) with its headquarters in Brussels.

In the early years the alliance expanded: Greece and Turkey joined in 1952, West Germany in 1955, and the military structure was formalized in 1950 with the creation of the Supreme Headquarters Allied Powers Europe (SHAPE) in 1951. The headquarters moved from London (1948‑1951) to Paris in April 1952.

During the Cold War, NATO served as a bulwark against the Soviet Union, especially after the formation of the Warsaw Pact in 1955. France’s withdrawal from the military structure in 1966 and participation in the Korean War reinforced the need for integrated defence.

With the end of the Cold War, the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989 opened the way for new missions. NATO intervened in Bosnia (1992‑1995) and, in 1999, in Yugoslavia (Kosovo), at the same time that former Soviet‑bloc countries – Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic – joined. In 2004, eight more former Warsaw Pact states became members.

Article 5 was invoked for the first time after the September 11 2001 attacks, leading NATO to lead the mission in Afghanistan. Since then the alliance has carried out operations in Libya (2011), sent instructors to Iraq, fought piracy and, after Russia’s annexation of Crimea in 2014, strengthened its presence in Eastern Europe. Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 accelerated expansion, culminating in Finland’s accession (2023) and Sweden’s accession (2024).

For Brazil, NATO represents a model of collective defence that influences national policy. Although not a member, the country participates in the Partnership for Peace, collaborates in joint exercises and follows the recommendation to allocate at least 2 % of GDP to defence, aligning with allies’ spending standards. This relationship strengthens the technological and operational capability of the Brazilian Armed Forces without creating direct defence obligations.

comoFuncionaIdeia: Military alliance where 32 countries commit to mutual defence through collective decisions and joint financing.
comoFunciona:
A NATO is based on the North Atlantic Treaty, signed on 4 April 1949. Article 5 obliges members to consider an attack on any one as an attack on all; it has been invoked only once, after the September 11, 2001 attacks. Article 4 allows consultations among the countries, already used five times, including by Turkey and Poland.

Strategic decisions are taken in meetings of heads of state and government, as well as in defence ministers' councils. The military command is centralized at the Supreme Headquarters Allied Powers Europe (SHAPE), led by the Supreme Allied Commander Europe (SACEUR), traditionally a U.S. general. This structure coordinates joint forces, peace missions and crisis responses.

Member countries fund their own defence with at least 2 % of GDP, as required by the treaty, and aim to reach 5 % by 2035. In addition, they contribute to a common budget that, in 2026, was about €5 billion, divided among the 32 members. This financing supports the headquarters in Brussels, the military headquarters and joint operations.

NATO carries out missions outside European territory, such as the International Security Assistance Force (ISAF) in Afghanistan, support to Iraq, anti‑piracy operations and the no‑fly zone over Libya in 2011. These interventions demonstrate the alliance’s ability to project power and cooperate with the UN.

Beyond the 32 members, the alliance maintains 21 countries in the Partnership for Peace and 15 in institutionalised dialogue programmes, expanding its global influence and facilitating cooperation with nations that are not yet full members.

vertentes.pensa: NATO guarantees the security of its members through Article 5, which treats an attack on one country as an attack on all.
vertentes.quemDefende: NATO member states (U.S., European countries, Canada) and governments that defend an international order based on alliances.
vertentes.porQue: Without NATO, no country would have the guarantee of immediate support against external aggression, which would weaken deterrence against adversary powers.
vertentes.criticas: It is criticized that the commitment can drag countries into foreign conflicts and that the alliance can be used as a pretext for military interventions.

vertentes.quemDefende: Russia and Russian media outlets (e.g., Meduza), as well as some analysts critical of Western policy.
vertentes.porQue: The alliance's presence near Russia's borders reduces Russia's strategic space and fuels the perception of encirclement, justifying its military stance.
vertentes.criticas: The expansion is considered by NATO supporters as a response to the sovereignty of countries seeking protection from Russian aggression.

vertentes.pensa: Members must meet spending targets (2 % of GDP) and the alliance heavily depends on US funding and direction.
vertentes.quemDefende: European governments that demand a larger US contribution and internal NATO critics who point out burden imbalances.
vertentes.porQue: Without a balanced financial contribution, NATO would not be able to maintain its operational capabilities; American leadership ensures strategic coherence.
vertentes.criticas: Spending targets are seen as burdensome for smaller economies and generate internal disputes, such as the 2025‑2026 crisis involving US threats to allies.

vertentes.pensa: NATO has been used to project Western power in conflicts outside its territory, such as Bosnia, Kosovo, Libya and Iraq.
vertentes.quemDefende: Defenders of Western foreign policy who view these actions as maintaining international order and protecting human rights.
vertentes.porQue: Interventions allow preventing humanitarian crises, containing regional aggressions, and demonstrating the alliance's joint-action capability.
vertentes.criticas: It is criticized that such interventions violate sovereignty, serve the strategic interests of members, and can generate prolonged instability.

cadeia.passo: NATO was created in 1949 as a collective defence alliance among the US, Canada and European countries, establishing Article 5 which considers an attack on one member as an attack on all.
The alliance developed military interoperability standards, training programmes and cyber‑security cooperation, which are offered to partner countries.
Brazil, although not a member, takes part in joint exercises and sends military personnel to NATO training courses, adopting some of these standards.
These interactions influence Brazilian defence policy, guiding equipment choices, spending requirements (2 % of GDP) and international cooperation strategies.
Consequently, the presence of NATO norms in Brazil affects how the country prepares for regional threats and collaborates in peace missions.
